The letters that turn into flags

Type GB with these letters and you do not get two tiles, you get a British flag, because building flags is what the regional indicator block is for. Country flag emoji are assembled from pairs of them. This generator puts a space between every letter so the pairs never form, which is the only dependable way to use the range as an alphabet. It starts at U+1F1E6, has one form per letter, and covers no digits.

The result is a row of wide lettered squares with a lot of air around them, which suits a Discord nickname or a one-line header far better than a sentence. Those inserted spaces have a cost: a six-letter word occupies eleven characters, and a tight field will trim or refuse it. Nothing has been restyled either. The letters are separate characters that were drawn to serve as flag halves and are being borrowed.

Also searched as: flag letters, regional indicator symbols, emoji letter tiles.

Where Regional Indicator text works, and where it does not

WorksRenders as coloured letter tiles on most platforms. Watch outTwo of these in a row that happen to form a country code turn into that country's flag — so 'GB' becomes 🇬🇧. Rarely what you wanted mid-word.

Regional Indicator questions

Why is there a space between every letter?

To stop flags forming. Two regional indicators sitting next to each other that spell a valid country code render as that country flag, so the word GRAB would open with a Greek flag and carry on in letters. The inserted space breaks every pair, at the cost of making the text noticeably longer than what you typed.

Can I still make an actual flag with these?

Yes. Delete the space between the two letters of a country code so the pair sits adjacent. That is all a flag emoji is, two of these tiles side by side, which is also why a system without the flag artwork simply shows you the two lettered squares instead of the picture.

Do capitals and lowercase come out differently?

No, there is one tile per letter and both cases point at it. That is a limit rather than a fault: the block exists to encode country codes, which are always written in capitals, so a lowercase set was never needed. Digits have no equivalent here either and stay as ordinary numbers.
